verses.hook: Why does Arjuna compare the warriors to rivers rushing to the sea?

views.text: As the swift currents of many rivers rush toward the sea alone, so the heroes of the human world, Bhīṣma and the others, enter the Lord's blazing mouths.
Reads the river image as entry under compulsion: currents from many channels have no say in reaching the sea, and so the heroes are swept into the flaming mouths.
Here Arjuna's delusion falls away: seeing the warriors already rushing to death, he grasps that the battle has the Lord's sanction and that he is only an instrument.
Noble kings who fought out of duty are like rivers merging willingly into the ocean; either way, all are moving swiftly toward their death.

verses.devanagari:
यथा प्रदीप्तं ज्वलनं पतङ्गा
विशन्ति नाशाय समृद्धवेगाः ।
तथैव नाशाय विशन्ति लोकास्-
तवापि वक्त्राणि समृद्धवेगाः॥
verses.transliteration:
yathā pradīptaṃ jvalanaṃ pataṅgā viśanti nāśāya samṛddhavegāḥ
tathaiva nāśāya viśanti lokāstavāpi vaktrāṇi samṛddhavegāḥ
verses.essence: As moths, with quickened speed, enter a blazing fire to their destruction — so do these beings, with quickened speed, enter your mouths to their destruction.
verses.translation: As moths hurriedly rush into a blazing fire for (their own) destruction, so also these creatures hurriedly rush into Thy mouths for (their own) destruction.

anvaya.form: past participle, masculine accusative singular (describing the fire)

anvaya.parts: समृद्ध (increased) + वेग (speed): those whose speed has grown
समृद्ध (increased) + वेग (speed): those whose speed has grown

verses.explanation: The second simile darkens the first: not rivers now but moths — pataṅgāḥ — flying into the flame on their own wings, their speed (samṛddha-vegāḥ) mistaken to the end about what the brightness is. Nāśāya, twice: *for destruction*. Śrīdhara draws the line between the two images: the rivers enter without choice, the moths enter knowingly. The same rushing, seen twice — the current that carries, then the desire that drives — and both end in the same mouths.
verses.connection: The darker twin of 11.28: the same motion, stripped of consolation.
verses.reflection: Then try the moth-reading on a craving: speed mistaken for desire's wisdom. Hold both readings.
verses.background: Arjuna finds words and they ascend from wonder to terror: all the gods in Your body, no beginning, middle, or end — then the blazing mouths, the worlds rushing in, the warriors of both armies streaming like rivers to the sea, like moths to flame, caught between the teeth. Trembling, he asks: who are You, of form so fierce, and what is Your purpose?
verses.hook: Why are some warriors like moths flying into a flame?

views.text: Takes lokāḥ as creatures in general rather than worlds, entering with ever-increasing haste for their own destruction.
The moth image is for deliberate entry: moths fly into the flame knowingly and with mounting speed, just as these people enter the mouths of their own will.
Those who fought from greed and self-interest are like moths lured blindly into fire, rushing ignorantly to their own destruction.

verses.devanagari:
लेलिह्यसे ग्रसमानः समन्ताल्-
लोकान्समग्रान्वदनैर्ज्वलद्भिः ।
तेजोभिरापूर्य जगत्समग्रं
भासस्तवोग्राः प्रतपन्ति विष्णो॥
verses.transliteration:
lelihyase grasamānaḥ samantāl- lokānsamagrānvadanairjvaladbhiḥ
tejobhirāpūrya jagatsamagraṃ bhāsastavogrāḥ pratapanti viṣṇo
verses.essence: You lick your lips, devouring all the worlds on every side with your flaming mouths. Your fierce rays fill the whole universe with radiance and scorch it, O Vishnu.
verses.translation: Thou lickest up, devouring all the worlds on every side with Thy flaming mouths. Thy fierce rays, filling the whole world with radiance, are burning, O Vishnu!

anvaya.form: verb, intensive, present, 2nd person singular (repeated, relished action)
present participle, middle, masculine nominative singular (devouring)
present participle, neuter instrumental plural (describing the mouths)

verses.explanation: Lelihyase — the intensive verb: licking, relishing, again and again. The hardest word in the chapter, because it adds appetite to destruction. Arjuna addresses this as *Vishnu*, and the commentators gloss the name by its root, the all-pervading: the fierce rays that scorch the universe have first filled it, so there is nowhere the burning does not reach. The one who fills every world is the one devouring them. The contradiction is now total, and unbearable.
verses.connection: The vision's nadir — beyond which only the demand of 11.31 is possible.
verses.reflection: When existence shows its devouring face, stay present anyway — the Preserver wears it too.
verses.background: Arjuna finds words and they ascend from wonder to terror: all the gods in Your body, no beginning, middle, or end — then the blazing mouths, the worlds rushing in, the warriors of both armies streaming like rivers to the sea, like moths to flame, caught between the teeth. Trembling, he asks: who are You, of form so fierce, and what is Your purpose?
verses.hook: What is Krishna's form doing to the worlds around it?

views.text: Reads lelihyase as 'you taste, you lick your lips' while swallowing creatures, and glosses Viṣṇu as the all-pervading One whose fierce rays scorch.
Pictures the licking as repeated and wrathful, lips wet with the kings' blood, and says this terrible form shows the boundless sovereignty Arjuna asked to see in 11.4.
Arjuna is seeing the Lord in his role as the all-devouring force of annihilation, swallowing enemies and allies alike in the coming battle, and he is petrified.

verses.devanagari:
आख्याहि मे को भवानुग्ररूपो
नमोऽस्तु ते देववर प्रसीद ।
विज्ञातुमिच्छामि भवन्तमाद्यं
न हि प्रजानामि तव प्रवृत्तिम्॥
verses.transliteration:
ākhyāhi me ko bhavānugrarūpo namo'stu te devavara prasīda
vijñātumicchāmi bhavantamādyaṃ na hi prajānāmi tava pravṛttim
verses.essence: Tell me who you are, O fierce of form! Salutation to you, best of gods — be gracious. I wish to know you, the Primal One, for I do not comprehend your working.
verses.translation: Tell me, who Thou art, so fierce of form. Salutations to Thee, O God Supreme: have mercy. I desire to know Thee, the original Being. I know not indeed Thy working.

anvaya.parts: उग्र (fierce) + रूप (form): one whose form is fierce
देव (god) + वर (best): the best among gods

verses.explanation: The hymn ends where honest prayer often does: in a question. Kaḥ bhavān — *who are you?* — asked by the man who has spent ten chapters being told. But doctrine named the being; the vision has shown the doing, and the doing is what he cannot square: na prajānāmi tava pravṛttim, I do not understand what you are *doing*. The next verse is the answer the whole Gita has been building toward.
verses.connection: The question that summons 11.32 — identity demanded at the point where understanding breaks.
verses.reflection: Bring your hardest question to the highest address today: Who are You, and what are You doing?
verses.background: Arjuna finds words and they ascend from wonder to terror: all the gods in Your body, no beginning, middle, or end — then the blazing mouths, the worlds rushing in, the warriors of both armies streaming like rivers to the sea, like moths to flame, caught between the teeth. Trembling, he asks: who are You, of form so fierce, and what is Your purpose?
verses.hook: What does a terrified Arjuna ask the fierce form?

views.text: Arjuna asks who this fierce form is, salutes him as foremost of gods and the Primal One who exists in the beginning, and seeks to know him fully, since he does not understand these actions.
Hears the question as one of purpose: why has the Lord taken this destroyer's form, and what does he mean to do? Arjuna asks him to say so and to take a pleasing form again.
Gives pravṛtti two senses: 'I do not know why you are acting like this', or 'I do not know even any account of one such as you'.
Bewildered by the spectacle he asked for, Arjuna now wants to know the very heart of God's nature and purpose: who are you, and what are you doing?

verses.speaker: श्रीभगवानुवाच
verses.devanagari:
कालोऽस्मि लोकक्षयकृत्प्रवृद्धो
लोकान्समाहर्तुमिह प्रवृत्तः ।
ऋतेऽपि त्वां न भविष्यन्ति सर्वे
येऽवस्थिताः प्रत्यनीकेषु योधाः॥
verses.transliteration:
kālo'smi lokakṣayakṛtpravṛddho lokānsamāhartumiha pravṛttaḥ
ṛte'pi tvāṃ na bhaviṣyanti sarve ye'vasthitāḥ pratyanīkeṣu yodhāḥ
verses.essence: The Blessed Lord says: I am Time, the destroyer of worlds, grown vast, engaged here in withdrawing the worlds. Even without you, none of these warriors arrayed in the opposing ranks shall remain.
verses.translation: I am the full-grown world-destroying Time, now engaged in destroying the worlds. Even without thee, none of the warriors arrayed in the hostile armies shall live.

anvaya.base: लोकक्षयकृत् · maker of the worlds' ruin
anvaya.parts: लोक (world) + क्षय (destruction) + कृत् (maker): the one who brings about the destruction of the worlds

anvaya.base: सम् + आ + √हृ · to draw together, withdraw

anvaya.parts: प्रति (against) + अनीक (army): the army facing one's own

verses.explanation: The self-naming: kālo 'smi — I am Time. Not a god *of* time; the thing itself, loka-kṣaya-kṛt pravṛddhaḥ, grown full and already gathering the worlds in. Then the clause that reframes Arjuna's entire crisis: ṛte 'pi tvām — *even without you* — these men will not survive; the war's outcome is not waiting on his conscience. The clause lifts authorship from his shoulders without lifting his duty. His choice was never whether they die. It is only what he will be while it happens.
verses.connection: The answer to 11.31 and to chapter 1 at once: the deaths Arjuna dreads causing are not his to cause.
verses.reflection: Let Time's self-naming resize one worry today: the outcome was never waiting on your anxiety.
verses.background: The answer that entered world history: I am Time, grown full, here to devour the worlds — even without you, these warriors will not survive. Therefore stand up, win glory, enjoy the kingdom: by Me they are already slain; be merely My instrument, O ambidextrous archer.
verses.hook: Who does Krishna say he is in this terrifying form?

views.text: The Lord is world-destroying Time, grown in stature to annihilate creatures; even without Arjuna, Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Karṇa and the others in the opposing armies, the source of his apprehension, will cease to exist.
Derives kāla from kalayati, 'he reckons': the Lord has counted out the end of these lives and, by his will alone, they will fall even without Arjuna's effort.
Spells out 'without you': even if you do not strike them, they are already seized by Me in the form of Time, and they will die.
Draws the lesson that Arjuna's instrumentality matters little: the warriors are doomed under the Lord's dispensation and Arjuna has already seen them dying.
Krishna is Time, which counts and ends every life; the enemy warriors will perish even without Arjuna, because that is part of the Lord's plan for the world.

verses.devanagari:
तस्मात्त्वमुत्तिष्ठ यशो लभस्व
जित्वा शत्रून् भुङ्क्ष्व राज्यं समृद्धम् ।
मयैवैते निहताः पूर्वमेव
निमित्तमात्रं भव सव्यसाचिन्॥
verses.transliteration:
tasmāttvamuttiṣṭha yaśo labhasva jitvā śatrūn bhuṅkṣva rājyaṃ samṛddham
mayaivaite nihatāḥ pūrvameva nimittamātraṃ bhava savyasācin
verses.essence: Therefore arise and win glory; conquering your foes, enjoy a prospering kingdom. By me they are slain already — be merely the instrument, O ambidextrous archer.
verses.translation: Therefore, stand up and obtain fame. Conquer the enemies and enjoy the unrivalled kingdom. Verily by Me have they been already slain; be thou a mere instrument, O Arjuna.

anvaya.form: pronoun in ablative singular, used as 'therefore'
imperative, 2nd person singular, middle voice (a command)
imperative, 2nd person singular, middle voice (a command)
past participle as adjective, neuter accusative singular
past passive participle, masculine nominative plural (slain)
noun, neuter, nominative singular (what you are to be)
anvaya.parts: निमित्त (instrument, occasion) + मात्र (mere): nothing more than the instrument

anvaya.base: सव्यसाचिन् · one who shoots with the left hand too
anvaya.parts: सव्य (left hand) + साचिन् (one who fixes arrows): who can draw the bow even with his left

verses.explanation: The chapter's command, hung on its strangest word: nihatāḥ pūrvam eva — slain *already*, a past participle spoken before an arrow flies. What Time has concluded, the field will merely transcribe. Hence the office offered to Arjuna: nimitta-mātram bhava, be merely the instrument — the occasion, the pen and not the author. The outcome is closed; the performance is open. The deed remains his to do, the death was never his to own, and what is left to choose is the spirit of the hand on the bow.
verses.connection: Converts 11.32's metaphysics into 2.37's old command — now with the weight of authorship lifted.
verses.reflection: Be the instrument once today: full effort, authorship surrendered — nimitta-matram in your own field.
verses.background: The answer that entered world history: I am Time, grown full, here to devour the worlds — even without you, these warriors will not survive. Therefore stand up, win glory, enjoy the kingdom: by Me they are already slain; be merely My instrument, O ambidextrous archer.
verses.hook: If the outcome is already decided, why should Arjuna still fight?

views.text: Arjuna should rise and win the fame of conquering Bhīṣma, Droṇa and others unconquerable even by gods, fame gained only by virtuous action; they are already killed by the Lord, and he is merely the instrument.
Those who sinned are already destroyed by the Lord; Arjuna is to be his instrument like a weapon in his hand. Savyasācin comes from √sac, to fasten: he can fix an arrow even with his left hand.
Takes 'they are slain, be the instrument and win glory' as the Lord's answer to Arjuna's earlier doubt in 2.6, that he did not know which side would prevail.

Softens 'slain' to 'as good as slain' by the Lord as Time before the fight begins, so Arjuna wins the fame of defeating Bhīṣma and Droṇa, whom even gods could not defeat, and the kingdom without strain.
God needs no one's help, but souls gain lasting good by serving his will; a chance to be his instrument is a special blessing that draws his grace.

verses.devanagari:
द्रोणं च भीष्मं च जयद्रथं च
कर्णं तथान्यानपि योधवीरान् ।
मया हतांस्त्वं जहि मा व्यथिष्ठा
युध्यस्व जेतासि रणे सपत्नान्॥
verses.transliteration:
droṇaṃ ca bhīṣmaṃ ca jayadrathaṃ ca karṇaṃ tathānyānapi yodhavīrān
mayā hatāṃstvaṃ jahi mā vyathiṣṭhā yudhyasva jetāsi raṇe sapatnān
verses.essence: Drona and Bhishma and Jayadratha, Karna, and the other warrior-heroes too — already slain by me: slay them. Do not waver. Fight! You shall conquer your rivals in battle.
verses.translation: Drona, Bhishma, Jayadratha, Karna and other brave warriors these are already slain by Me: do thou kill; be not distressed with fear; fight and thou shalt conquer thy enemies in battle.

anvaya.base: जयद्रथ · Jayadratha, king of the Sindhus

anvaya.parts: योध (warrior) + वीर (hero): warriors who are heroes

anvaya.form: past passive participle, masculine accusative plural (already slain)
aorist, 2nd person singular, middle (used with मा: 'do not')
imperative, 2nd person singular, middle voice (a command)
periphrastic future, first part (agent noun, nominative singular)
verb, present, 2nd person singular (completes the future: 'you will conquer')

verses.explanation: The names Arjuna could not face in chapter 1 are spoken back to him one by one — Drona his teacher, Bhishma his grandsire — each already filed under mayā hatān, slain by me. The paradoxical imperative follows: *you* slay the already-slain. And mā vyathiṣṭhāḥ — the same root as the worlds' trembling — do not tremble. Then a promise, flatly given: jetāsi, you will win.
verses.connection: Applies 11.33 to the exact faces of 1.26: the beloved enemies, pre-decided.
verses.reflection: Face one named fear today knowing the issue is already settled above your pay grade — and act.
verses.background: The answer that entered world history: I am Time, grown full, here to devour the worlds — even without you, these warriors will not survive. Therefore stand up, win glory, enjoy the kingdom: by Me they are already slain; be merely My instrument, O ambidextrous archer.
verses.hook: Can even the strongest warriors survive what God has willed?

views.text: Explains why these four are named: each was a real ground for doubt — Droṇa's divine weapons, Bhīṣma's death only at will, the curse guarding Jayadratha's head, Karṇa's unerring spear from Indra.

These men have broken dharma by siding with Duryodhana and are chosen by the Lord for destruction; so Arjuna need not agonise over right and wrong or pity them, and there is no cruelty in slaying them.
Reads 'mā vyathiṣṭhāḥ' as 'do not grieve', and sees the whole verse as dissolving the doubt of 2.6 about which side is weightier: victory is certain.
No boon or protection can save those God wills to fall, yet he lets Arjuna win the glory, because God loves to glorify his devotees; likewise our effort plus his grace conquers inner enemies.

verses.speaker: सञ्जय उवाच
verses.devanagari:
एतच्छ्रुत्वा वचनं केशवस्य
कृताञ्जलिर्वेपमानः किरीटी ।
नमस्कृत्वा भूय एवाह कृष्णं
सगद्गदं भीतभीतः प्रणम्य॥
verses.transliteration:
etacchrutvā vacanaṃ keśavasya kṛtāñjalirvepamānaḥ kirīṭī
namaskṛtvā bhūya evāha kṛṣṇaṃ sagadgadaṃ bhītabhītaḥ praṇamya
verses.essence: Sanjaya says: hearing this word of Keshava, the crowned one, trembling and with palms joined, bowed down; terrified, prostrating, he spoke to Krishna again in a choked voice.
verses.translation: Having heard that speech of Lord Krishna, Arjuna, with joined palms, trembling, prostrating himself, again addressed Krishna, in a choked voice, bowing down, overwhelmed with fear.

anvaya.base: केशव · Keshava, a name of Krishna
कृताञ्जलि · one who has joined his palms
anvaya.parts: कृत (made) + अञ्जलि (hollow of joined palms): one who has folded his hands

anvaya.form: present participle, middle, masculine nominative singular (trembling)
adverb (accusative form, describing how he spoke)
anvaya.parts: स (with) + गद्गद (stammer): with a faltering voice

anvaya.form: adjective, masculine, nominative singular (repeated for intensity)
anvaya.parts: भीत (afraid) + भीत (afraid): afraid again and again

verses.explanation: Sanjaya breaks in to show us what doctrine cannot: the body of the listener. Vepamānaḥ, trembling; sa-gadgadam, the voice catching and breaking; bhīta-bhītaḥ, fear upon fear, struck by it again and again. The hero's epithet kirīṭī — the diademed — stands in deliberate contrast to the prostrate figure wearing it.
verses.connection: The narrative pulse-check before Arjuna's second hymn (11.36–46): awe registered in flesh and voice.
verses.reflection: Let your body pray when words fail — joined palms, bowed head, a breaking voice are all liturgy.
verses.background: Arjuna, trembling and prostrating, breaks into the Gita's great hymn: salutations in front, behind, on every side, O All. Then the most human turn — he begs pardon for every past familiarity, for 'O Krishna, O friend' spoken in play and at meals, not knowing this greatness — and pleads to see again the gentle four-armed form, for he cannot bear this one.
verses.hook: How does Arjuna respond when Krishna calls him to act?

views.text: Explains gadgada: when fear brings sorrow or love brings joy, the throat chokes and the eyes fill, and speech grows indistinct. Sañjaya reports this hoping Dhṛtarāṣṭra, seeing defeat coming, would make peace.
Traces the choking voice to a mix of fear and joy overwhelming Arjuna, and reads bhīta-bhītaḥ as 'more afraid than the afraid' as he bows low.
Sanjaya calls Arjuna the crowned one, recalling Indra's gift, and through the crown hints to Dhṛtarāṣṭra that his sons will lose the throne to the Pandavas.

verses.speaker: अर्जुन उवाच
verses.devanagari:
स्थाने हृषीकेश तव प्रकीर्त्या
जगत्प्रहृष्यत्यनुरज्यते च ।
रक्षांसि भीतानि दिशो द्रवन्ति
सर्वे नमस्यन्ति च सिद्धसङ्घाः॥
verses.transliteration:
sthāne hṛṣīkeśa tava prakīrtyā jagatprahṛṣyatyanurajyate ca
rakṣāṃsi bhītāni diśo dravanti sarve namasyanti ca siddhasaṅghāḥ
verses.essence: Arjuna says: rightly, Hrishikesha, does the world rejoice and delight in your praise; the rakshasas flee in terror to every quarter, and all the hosts of siddhas bow.
verses.translation: It is meet, O Krishna, that the world delights and rejoices in Thy praise; demons fly in fear to all quarters and the hosts of the perfected ones bow to Thee.

anvaya.parts: हृषीक (sense) + ईश (lord): master of the senses
सिद्ध (perfected one) + सङ्घ (host): crowds of perfected beings

verses.explanation: Sthāne — 'rightly so', 'it is fitting': Arjuna's second hymn opens not with terror but with assent. Something has settled. The same form that routs the demonic delights the world; the response splits each being along its own grain. He is learning to praise what he could not, minutes ago, even comprehend.
verses.connection: The hymn of reconciliation begins: terror metabolizing into worship.
verses.reflection: Say 'rightly so' once today — sthane — assenting to a vastness you spent yesterday resisting.
verses.background: Arjuna, trembling and prostrating, breaks into the Gita's great hymn: salutations in front, behind, on every side, O All. Then the most human turn — he begs pardon for every past familiarity, for 'O Krishna, O friend' spoken in play and at meals, not knowing this greatness — and pleads to see again the gentle four-armed form, for he cannot bear this one.
verses.hook: Why do some rejoice and others flee before Krishna?

views.text: Offers a second sense of sthāne: the Lord is the proper object of this joy and attraction, because he is the Self of all beings and the friend of all.
The rejoicing world is the gathering of gods, gandharvas, siddhas and others come to watch the battle, delighted on beholding him by his grace; the siddhas who bow are those well-disposed to him.
Not only Arjuna but the whole world rejoices at the praise of so wondrous and devotee-loving a Lord; sthāne means it is fitting, no wonder at all.
As subjects praise a rightful king, enemies flee him and ministers serve him, so it is fitting that the world glorifies the Lord, demons fear him and saints adore him.

verses.devanagari:
कस्माच्च ते न नमेरन्महात्मन्
गरीयसे ब्रह्मणोऽप्यादिकर्त्रे ।
अनन्त देवेश जगन्निवास
त्वमक्षरं सदसत्तत्परं यत्॥
verses.transliteration:
kasmācca te na nameranmahātman garīyase brahmaṇo'pyādikartre
ananta deveśa jagannivāsa tvamakṣaraṃ sadasattatparaṃ yat
verses.essence: And why should they not bow to you, O great Self — greater even than Brahma, and his first creator? Infinite Lord of gods, dwelling of the universe: you are the imperishable — being, non-being, and what is beyond both.
verses.translation: And why should they not, O great Soul, bow to Thee Who art greater (than all else), the primal cause even of the Creator (Brahma), O Infinite Being, O Lord of the gods, O Abode of the universe; Thou art the imperishable, the Being, the non-being and That which is the supreme (that which is beyond the Being and the non-being).

anvaya.parts: महा (great) + आत्मन् (self): the great Self

anvaya.form: noun, masculine, ablative or genitive singular (than / of)

anvaya.parts: आदि (first) + कर्तृ (maker): the first maker

anvaya.form: adjective as noun, masculine, vocative singular (calling Krishna)

anvaya.parts: देव (god) + ईश (lord): the lord of the gods
जगत् (world) + निवास (dwelling): one in whom the world dwells

anvaya.form: adjective as noun, neuter, nominative singular

verses.explanation: The logic of worship made explicit: garīyase brahmaṇo 'py ādi-kartre — weightier than the world's own maker; bowing is simply accuracy. And the metaphysical reach of the line: sat, asat, tat-param yat — what is, what is not, and the third thing past both, for which philosophy keeps a respectful blank.
verses.connection: Grounds 11.36's universal homage in ontology: nothing stands outside what is being praised.
verses.reflection: Bow once today simply because bowing is accuracy before what is greater.
verses.background: Arjuna, trembling and prostrating, breaks into the Gita's great hymn: salutations in front, behind, on every side, O All. Then the most human turn — he begs pardon for every past familiarity, for 'O Krishna, O friend' spoken in play and at meals, not knowing this greatness — and pleads to see again the gentle four-armed form, for he cannot bear this one.
verses.hook: Why should every being, even the creator, bow to Krishna?

views.text: Being and non-being are only the limiting adjuncts of the Imperishable, which is spoken of as both by courtesy but in truth transcends both — the Akṣara of 8.11.
Akṣara here is the individual self, which never perishes; sat and asat are matter as effect and as cause; 'what is beyond' is the liberated self. The Lord is all these as their Self.
Asat because the Absolute never becomes an object of perception; beyond both because it is realised only when the knowing of existent and non-existent itself disappears.
Creation comes from, rests in and returns to God; he is both manifest and unmanifest yet beyond both, and is even Brahmā's grandsire, so all rightly bow to him.

verses.devanagari:
त्वमादिदेवः पुरुषः पुराणस्-
त्वमस्य विश्वस्य परं निधानम् ।
वेत्तासि वेद्यं च परं च धाम
त्वया ततं विश्वमनन्तरूप॥
verses.transliteration:
tvamādidevaḥ puruṣaḥ purāṇastvamasya viśvasya paraṃ nidhānam
vettāsi vedyaṃ ca paraṃ ca dhāma tvayā tataṃ viśvamanantarūpa
verses.essence: You are the first of gods, the ancient Person; you are the supreme resting-place of all this. You are the knower and the known and the highest abode. By you the universe is pervaded, O infinite form!
verses.translation: Thou art the primal God, the ancient Purusha, the supreme refuge of this universe, the knower, the knowable and the supreme Abode. By Thee is the universe pervaded, O Being of infinite forms.

anvaya.parts: आदि (first) + देव (god): the god at the beginning

anvaya.form: gerundive, neuter nominative singular (to be known)
past participle, neuter nominative singular (spread through)

anvaya.parts: अनन्त (endless) + रूप (form): one whose forms have no end

verses.explanation: The hymn gathers the Upanishadic vocabulary into one address — and hides its sharpest line in the middle: vettā asi vedyaṁ ca, you are the knower *and* the known. The seeking subject and the sought object, both him. Every search, this implies, is God looking for God — including the search trembling on this chariot.
verses.connection: Deepens 11.37: the duality of seeker and goal dissolved inside the one being addressed.
verses.reflection: Mid-search today, remember: the knower and the known are one — your seeking is being met.
verses.background: Arjuna, trembling and prostrating, breaks into the Gita's great hymn: salutations in front, behind, on every side, O All. Then the most human turn — he begs pardon for every past familiarity, for 'O Krishna, O friend' spoken in play and at meals, not knowing this greatness — and pleads to see again the gentle four-armed form, for he cannot bear this one.
verses.hook: Is there anything that Krishna himself comes from?

refs.note: Brahmā praises Krishna as the original Lord, full of knowledge and bliss, without origin yet the cause of all causes.
Says true knowledge is what helps us know God, showing Krishna as the object of all knowing.

views.text: Nidhāna is where the whole universe comes to rest at dissolution; param dhāma is the supreme state of Viṣṇu; the knower is he who knows all that is to be known.
The Lord is the supreme foundation of a universe that is his body, he being its Self; he is every knower and every object known, and the goal to be reached.
Like clay to the pot, the world comes from the Lord and dissolves in him, so he is its material cause; as the all-knowing knower he is also its efficient cause.
Everything has a cause, even Vishnu, who expands from Krishna, but Krishna is the causeless first cause; he is both the all-knower and the one true object of knowledge.

verses.devanagari:
वायुर्यमोऽग्निर्वरुणः शशाङ्कः
प्रजापतिस्त्वं प्रपितामहश्च ।
नमो नमस्तेऽस्तु सहस्रकृत्वः
पुनश्च भूयोऽपि नमो नमस्ते॥
verses.transliteration:
vāyuryamo'gnirvaruṇaḥ śaśāṅkaḥ prajāpatistvaṃ prapitāmahaśca
namo namaste'stu sahasrakṛtvaḥ punaśca bhūyo'pi namo namaste
verses.essence: You are Vayu, Yama, Agni, Varuna, the moon; Prajapati are you, and the great-grandsire. Salutation, salutation to you a thousand times — and again, even more: salutation, salutation!
verses.translation: Thou art Vayu, Yama, Agni, Varuna, the moon, the Creator, and the great-grandfather. Salutations, salutations unto Thee, a thousand times, and again salutations, salutations unto Thee.

anvaya.base: वरुण · Varuna, god of the waters

anvaya.parts: शश (hare) + अङ्क (mark): the one marked with a hare, the moon
प्रजा (creatures) + पति (lord): lord of all beings
प्र (before, further) + पितामह (grandfather): grandfather's father
सहस्र (thousand) + कृत्वस् (times): a thousandfold

verses.explanation: The old gods are folded in by name — wind, death, fire, waters, moon — and then language gives up its other function and becomes pure gesture: namo namas te... punaś ca bhūyo 'pi namo namas te. Four salutations in two lines, the words repeating because nothing else is left for them to do. This is what speech sounds like when it has finished meaning and started bowing.
verses.connection: The hymn's crest: vocabulary exhausted, repetition becomes the prayer.
verses.reflection: Let language become gesture once today: repeat one salutation until it stops meaning and starts bowing.
verses.background: Arjuna, trembling and prostrating, breaks into the Gita's great hymn: salutations in front, behind, on every side, O All. Then the most human turn — he begs pardon for every past familiarity, for 'O Krishna, O friend' spoken in play and at meals, not knowing this greatness — and pleads to see again the gentle four-armed form, for he cannot bear this one.
verses.hook: How can Krishna be the wind, fire, moon and the other gods?

views.text: Prajāpati is glossed as Kaśyapa and the other lords of creatures, and the Great-grandfather as the father even of Brahmā; the repeated salutations show Arjuna's dissatisfaction with a few, from abundant reverence and devotion.
Works out 'great-grandfather': the Prajāpatis father all creatures, Brahmā fathers the Prajāpatis, and the Lord, father even of Brahmā, is great-grandsire of all. The gods' names all name him.
Naming Vāyu and the rest marks the Lord as the Self of all deities; the repeated salutations show Arjuna, brimming with devotion and faith, finding no satisfaction in bowing only once.
As sweets of many shapes are all sugar and ornaments are all gold, the one God shines in every deity; God is all the gods, but the gods are not God.

verses.devanagari:
नमः पुरस्तादथ पृष्ठतस्ते
नमोऽस्तु ते सर्वत एव सर्व ।
अनन्तवीर्यामितविक्रमस्त्वं
सर्वं समाप्नोषि ततोऽसि सर्वः॥
verses.transliteration:
namaḥ purastādatha pṛṣṭhataste namo'stu te sarvata eva sarva
anantavīryāmitavikramastvaṃ sarvaṃ samāpnoṣi tato'si sarvaḥ
verses.essence: Salutation to you from the front and from behind; salutation to you on every side, O All! Of infinite might and immeasurable strength, you pervade everything — and therefore you are everything.
verses.translation: Salutations to Thee, in front and behind! Salutations to Thee on every side! O All!! Thou infinite in power and prowess, pervadest all; wherefore Thou art all.

anvaya.meaning: of endless power and boundless might
anvaya.parts: अनन्त (endless) + वीर्य (strength) + अमित (unmeasured) + विक्रम (valour): one whose strength is endless and valour measureless

verses.explanation: Geometry returns one last time, reconciled: bowing front, back, every side — the directions Arjuna lost in 11.25 are restored as so many angles of homage. And the hymn closes its argument with a syllogism of two words: samāpnoṣi, you fill everything; tato 'si sarvaḥ — *therefore you are everything*. Pervasion, thought through, is identity.
verses.connection: Completes the praise-hymn — and pivots to what total presence implies about an old friendship.
verses.reflection: Bow in all directions inwardly once — front, behind, every side — there is no away from this.
verses.background: Arjuna, trembling and prostrating, breaks into the Gita's great hymn: salutations in front, behind, on every side, O All. Then the most human turn — he begs pardon for every past familiarity, for 'O Krishna, O friend' spoken in play and at meals, not knowing this greatness — and pleads to see again the gentle four-armed form, for he cannot bear this one.
verses.hook: Why does Arjuna bow to Krishna from every side?

views.text: Strength (vīrya) and heroism (vikrama) are distinguished, since one may have strength yet little heroism; the Lord has both infinitely and pervades the universe by his single Self, so he is All: nothing exists without him.
Because all beings, sentient and insentient, are the Lord's body and modes, every word naming them truly names him; pervading them as their Self is the reason he 'is all'.
The Lord pervades everything within and without as gold pervades bracelets and earrings made from it; so he is all, and salutation is due on every side.
Asks how the all-pervading could have a front or back: in his extreme devotion Arjuna imagined sides to the Lord and bowed toward every one.
Overwhelmed by Krishna's infinite strength and power, Arjuna bows to him in every direction, again and again, since he pervades everything.

verses.devanagari:
सखेति मत्वा प्रसभं यदुक्तं
हे कृष्ण हे यादव हे सखेति ।
अजानता महिमानं तवेदं
मया प्रमादात्प्रणयेन वापि॥
verses.transliteration:
sakheti matvā prasabhaṃ yaduktaṃ he kṛṣṇa he yādava he sakheti
ajānatā mahimānaṃ tavedaṃ mayā pramādātpraṇayena vāpi
verses.essence: Whatever I said rashly, thinking of you as friend — 'O Krishna! O Yadava! O comrade!' — unknowing of this your greatness, out of carelessness or even out of love —
verses.translation: Whatever I have presumptuously said from carelessness or love, addressing Thee as O Krishna! O Yadava! O Friend! regarding Thee merely as a friend, unknowing of this, Thy greatness.

anvaya.form: past passive participle, neuter nominative singular (said)
present participle, masculine instrumental singular (by one unaware)
noun, masculine, ablative singular (from, because of)

verses.explanation: The most human turn in the chapter: Arjuna replaying decades of casual address — hey Krishna, hey Yadava — every easy word now enormous in retrospect. His honesty about the cause is exact: pramādāt praṇayena vāpi, from heedlessness *or from love*. He cannot tell which, because in friendship they are the same thing.
verses.connection: Begins the apology (11.41–44): intimacy auditing itself before the revealed infinite.
verses.reflection: Review your casual words to those you love — and let retrospect deepen, not poison, the affection.
verses.background: Arjuna, trembling and prostrating, breaks into the Gita's great hymn: salutations in front, behind, on every side, O All. Then the most human turn — he begs pardon for every past familiarity, for 'O Krishna, O friend' spoken in play and at meals, not knowing this greatness — and pleads to see again the gentle four-armed form, for he cannot bear this one.
verses.hook: Why does Arjuna regret calling Krishna his friend?

refs.note: The Lord declares that he alone exists and nothing is beyond or higher than him, the supremacy Arjuna now realises.
Says Om is the Lord's own manifestation and that he is greater than the greatest.
Calls God the highest and ultimate person, supporting Arjuna's new awareness of Krishna's greatness.

views.text: Praṇaya is the familiarity born of love; Arjuna wrongly took the Lord for a friend of his own age. Notes too that neuter idam is joined to masculine mahimānam by a change of gender.
Arjuna had taken Krishna for an ordinary friend; the form 'he sakheti' is an archaic sandhi of the seers. He begins asking forgiveness, completed in the next verse.
Deep love makes a devotee forget the Beloved's majesty. Now aware of Krishna's supremacy, Arjuna fears his casual familiarity was disrespectful and asks pardon.

verses.devanagari:
यच्चावहासार्थमसत्कृतोऽसि
विहारशय्यासनभोजनेषु ।
एकोऽथवाप्यच्युत तत्समक्षं
तत्क्षामये त्वामहमप्रमेयम्॥
verses.transliteration:
yaccāvahāsārthamasatkṛto'si vihāraśayyāsanabhojaneṣu
eko'thavāpyacyuta tatsamakṣaṃ tatkṣāmaye tvāmahamaprameyam
verses.essence: — and however I slighted you in jest: at play, in bed, seated or at meals, alone or before others, O unshakable one — for that I beg forgiveness of you, the immeasurable.
verses.translation: In whatever way I may have insulted Thee for the sake of fun, while at play, reposing, sitting or at meals, when alone (with Thee), O Krishna, or in company that I implore Thee, immeasurable one, to forgive.

anvaya.form: relative pronoun, neuter (that, in whatever way)

anvaya.base: अवहासार्थ · for the purpose of jest
anvaya.parts: अवहास (jest) + अर्थ (purpose): for the sake of fun

anvaya.base: विहार, शय्या, आसन, भोजन · play, bed, seat, meal
anvaya.parts: विहार (play, walking) + शय्या (bed) + आसन (seat) + भोजन (meal): in play, on the bed, at sitting and at meals
तत् (them) + समक्ष (before the eyes): in the sight of those others

verses.explanation: The inventory of intimacy: play, bed, seat, table — the four geographies of friendship, every one now reviewed under infinite light. The verse holds the Gita's tenderest paradox: only a God who had truly been a *friend* — teased, jostled, kept waiting at dinner — could need this apology. The incarnation was so complete it accumulated inside jokes.
verses.connection: Completes 11.41's confession with its domestic particulars — the divinity of the shared meal.
verses.reflection: Apologize today for one old carelessness that only love would even remember.
verses.background: Arjuna, trembling and prostrating, breaks into the Gita's great hymn: salutations in front, behind, on every side, O All. Then the most human turn — he begs pardon for every past familiarity, for 'O Krishna, O friend' spoken in play and at meals, not knowing this greatness — and pleads to see again the gentle four-armed form, for he cannot bear this one.
verses.hook: What careless moments with Krishna does Arjuna ask pardon for?

refs.note: Calls Vāsudeva, Krishna, the ultimate Supreme Lord.
States there is no god higher than Keśava, Krishna.

views.text: Glosses aprameya as 'beyond the means of knowledge': the offences were committed against one whom no measure can grasp, and Arjuna asks pardon for all of them.

Ekaḥ means alone with Krishna, without the other companions; tat-samakṣam means in front of those teasing friends. Arjuna asks pardon for the whole set of faults, before One whose power is unthinkable.
Arjuna recalls jokes, meals and rest shared with Krishna in loving intimacy, unaware of his supreme position, and now begs forgiveness for any offence.

verses.devanagari:
पितासि लोकस्य चराचरस्य
त्वमस्य पूज्यश्च गुरुर्गरीयान् ।
न त्वत्समोऽस्त्यभ्यधिकः कुतोऽन्यो
लोकत्रयेऽप्यप्रतिमप्रभाव॥
verses.transliteration:
pitāsi lokasya carācarasya tvamasya pūjyaśca gururgarīyān
na tvatsamo'styabhyadhikaḥ kuto'nyo lokatraye'pyapratimaprabhāva
verses.essence: You are the father of this world, of the moving and unmoving; you are its object of worship, its weightiest guru. None equals you — how could any be greater, O power without likeness in all three worlds?
verses.translation: Thou art the Father of this world, moving and unmoving. Thou art to be adored by this world, Thou, the greatest Guru; (for) none there exists who is equal to Thee; how then could there be another superior to Thee in the three worlds, O Being of unequalled power?

anvaya.parts: चर (moving) + अचर (unmoving): all that moves and does not move

anvaya.form: gerundive, masculine nominative singular (to be worshipped)

anvaya.parts: त्वत् (you) + सम (equal): one equal to you
लोक (world) + त्रय (triad): the three worlds
अ (not) + प्रतिमा (likeness, measure) + प्रभाव (power): one whose power has no equal

verses.explanation: The relationship is formally re-founded: pitā, pūjyaḥ, gurur garīyān — father, worshipful, weightiest teacher. The friend has not been lost but re-housed inside something vaster. And the logic of incomparability: where nothing is even equal, 'greater' is not a possibility but a grammatical error.
verses.connection: The apology resolves into right relation: friendship preserved, but re-ordered under reverence.
verses.reflection: Re-house a beloved relationship inside reverence today — friend, and father, and teacher at once.
verses.background: Arjuna, trembling and prostrating, breaks into the Gita's great hymn: salutations in front, behind, on every side, O All. Then the most human turn — he begs pardon for every past familiarity, for 'O Krishna, O friend' spoken in play and at meals, not knowing this greatness — and pleads to see again the gentle four-armed form, for he cannot bear this one.
verses.hook: Is there anyone equal to or greater than Krishna?

refs.note: Says no one is equal to God and no one is greater, the very truth Arjuna voices here.
Says the Lord placed Vedic knowledge in the heart of Brahmā, the first teacher, making him the supreme guru.

views.text: None can equal the Lord because there cannot be two Gods: with many independent rulers the world's order would collapse. He is greater than a teacher, being teacher even of Hiraṇyagarbha.
The Lord is father, teacher and most worthy of reverence; no being equals him in compassion and his other attributes, so none could surpass him.
Krishna is the father of all fathers and the teacher of all teachers, since even Brahmā received the Vedas from him; Arjuna recognises him as the Lord of the Vedas, without equal.

verses.devanagari:
तस्मात्प्रणम्य प्रणिधाय कायं
प्रसादये त्वामहमीशमीड्यम् ।
पितेव पुत्रस्य सखेव सख्युः
प्रियः प्रियायार्हसि देव सोढुम्॥
verses.transliteration:
tasmātpraṇamya praṇidhāya kāyaṃ prasādaye tvāmahamīśamīḍyam
piteva putrasya sakheva sakhyuḥ priyaḥ priyāyārhasi deva soḍhum
verses.essence: Therefore, bowing and prostrating my body, I ask grace of you, the Lord, the praiseworthy. As a father with a son, a friend with a friend, a lover with the beloved — so should you bear with me, O God.
verses.translation: Therefore, bowing down, prostrating my body, I crave Thy forgiveness, O adorable Lord. As a father forgives his son, a friend his (dear) friend, a lover his beloved, even so shouldst Thou forgive me, O God.

anvaya.form: pronoun in ablative singular, used as 'therefore'

anvaya.base: प्र + नि + √धा · to lay down, place
प्र + √सद् · to be pleased (causative: to propitiate)

anvaya.form: gerundive, masculine accusative singular (to be praised)

verses.explanation: Having confessed the presumption of intimacy, Arjuna does something braver: he asks for it back. Three analogies, ascending in tenderness — father-son, friend-friend, lover-beloved — each a relation in which faults are not merely excused but *absorbed*. He is asking the Infinite to keep loving him the small way, the personal way. It is the boldest request in the chapter, bolder than asking to see the form.
verses.connection: The apology's astonishing conclusion: forgiveness sought in the very currency of the offense — closeness.
verses.reflection: Ask to be borne with as lover bears beloved — and bear with someone else the same way today.
verses.background: Arjuna, trembling and prostrating, breaks into the Gita's great hymn: salutations in front, behind, on every side, O All. Then the most human turn — he begs pardon for every past familiarity, for 'O Krishna, O friend' spoken in play and at meals, not knowing this greatness — and pleads to see again the gentle four-armed form, for he cannot bear this one.
verses.hook: How does Arjuna hope Krishna will forgive him?

views.text: Bowing and laying his body fully down, Arjuna seeks to propitiate the adorable Lord, asking him to bear with his faults as a father bears a son's, a friend a friend's, a lover a beloved's.
Reads priyaḥ priyāyāḥ as 'you, dear to me, should bear with me, who am dear to you': as a father or friend forgives when entreated, so should the most compassionate Lord.
Each image is one of bearing another's fault: a father out of compassion, a friend as a kinsman without motive, a lover for the beloved's sake. Prostrating like a staff, Arjuna asks the same.
Arjuna's familiar dealings were not offences but signs of loving friendship, which God values more than formal respect; yet a devotee is humble, so he asks pardon.

verses.devanagari:
अदृष्टपूर्वं हृषितोऽस्मि दृष्ट्वा
भयेन च प्रव्यथितं मनो मे ।
तदेव मे दर्शय देव रूपं
प्रसीद देवेश जगन्निवास॥
verses.transliteration:
adṛṣṭapūrvaṃ hṛṣito'smi dṛṣṭvā bhayena ca pravyathitaṃ mano me
tadeva me darśaya deva rūpaṃ prasīda deveśa jagannivāsa
verses.essence: Having seen what was never seen before, I am thrilled — and my mind is shaken with fear. Show me that other form, O God; be gracious, Lord of gods, dwelling of the universe.
verses.translation: I am delighted, having seen what has never been seen before; and yet my mind is distressed with fear. Show me that (previous) form only, O God; have mercy, O God of gods, O Abode of the universe.

anvaya.form: adjective as noun, neuter, accusative singular (object)
anvaya.parts: अ (not) + दृष्ट (seen) + पूर्व (before): never seen before
देव (god) + ईश (lord): the lord of the gods
जगत् (world) + निवास (dwelling): one in whom the world dwells

verses.explanation: Both truths in one breath: hṛṣito 'smi — I am exhilarated — *and* my mind shakes with fear; the vision was gift and wound at once. Then the request that reverses the chapter: tad eva me darśaya rūpam — show me *that* form, the old one, the friend's form he knew before the sky split open. Having seen everything, Arjuna asks for the face he loves.
verses.connection: The counter-request to 11.3: the petition to close what he begged to open.
verses.reflection: Permit both at once today: thrilled and afraid. Then ask, without shame, for the gentler face.
verses.background: Arjuna, trembling and prostrating, breaks into the Gita's great hymn: salutations in front, behind, on every side, O All. Then the most human turn — he begs pardon for every past familiarity, for 'O Krishna, O friend' spoken in play and at meals, not knowing this greatness — and pleads to see again the gentle four-armed form, for he cannot bear this one.
verses.hook: Why does Arjuna, thrilled yet afraid, ask for the earlier form?

views.text: The cosmic form had never been seen by Arjuna or by anyone; 'that very form' is the form of his friend, which he now asks to see again.
The cosmic vision overwhelms and terrifies an ordinary man, but to a yogi it is strengthening and uplifting; Arjuna asks for the form Krishna wears as his friend.
Devotion of awe toward God's majesty keeps distance; intimate devotion, as friend, parent or beloved, is far sweeter. Arjuna, a devotee in friendship, longs for Krishna's familiar form again.

verses.devanagari:
किरीटिनं गदिनं चक्रहस्त-
मिच्छामि त्वां द्रष्टुमहं तथैव ।
तेनैव रूपेण चतुर्भुजेन
सहस्रबाहो भव विश्वमूर्ते॥
verses.transliteration:
kirīṭinaṃ gadinaṃ cakrahastamicchāmi tvāṃ draṣṭumahaṃ tathaiva
tenaiva rūpeṇa caturbhujena sahasrabāho bhava viśvamūrte
verses.essence: Crowned, with mace and discus in hand — thus I wish to see you, just as before. Take again that four-armed shape, O thousand-armed, O form of all!
verses.translation: I desire to see Thee as before, crowned, bearing a mace, with the discus in hand, in Thy former form only, having four arms, O thousand-armed, Cosmic Form (Being).

anvaya.parts: चक्र (discus) + हस्त (hand): one who has a discus in his hand
चतुर् (four) + भुज (arm): that which has four arms
सहस्र (thousand) + बाहु (arm): one who has a thousand arms

anvaya.base: विश्वमूर्ति · whose form is the universe
anvaya.parts: विश्व (all, universe) + मूर्ति (form, body): one whose body is the universe

verses.explanation: The negotiation is touching in its precision: not even the two-armed charioteer yet, but the caturbhuja — Vishnu's four-armed majesty, divinity at a scale a devotee can stand before. Arjuna addresses the thousand-armed and asks it to consent to four. Worship, it turns out, needs a form sized for love.
verses.connection: The step-down request: from the all-form to the adorable form — fulfilled across 11.47–51.
verses.reflection: It is allowed to ask the infinite for a form your love can stand before — ask today.
verses.background: Arjuna, trembling and prostrating, breaks into the Gita's great hymn: salutations in front, behind, on every side, O All. Then the most human turn — he begs pardon for every past familiarity, for 'O Krishna, O friend' spoken in play and at meals, not knowing this greatness — and pleads to see again the gentle four-armed form, for he cannot bear this one.
verses.hook: Which form of Krishna does Arjuna now ask to see?

refs.note: Describes Krishna in four-armed form smiling at Arjuna when Aśvatthāmā was brought before Draupadī, another time Arjuna saw that form.

views.text: The request is to withdraw the cosmic form and appear again as the son of Vasudeva, crowned and four-armed; 'thousand-armed' names only the form now before him.

The words 'as before' show Arjuna had always seen Krishna crowned and bearing mace and discus; the earlier description of crowns in the vision is reconciled with this as the same gentle form now seen blazing.
A warning to seekers who demand the highest experiences at once: without patience they cannot bear the power that surges in, as Arjuna could not bear the cosmic form.
Arjuna is not drawn to infinite opulence; he wants the Lord in a form he can relate to as a friend, and his request shows the four-armed and two-armed forms are one.

verses.speaker: श्रीभगवानुवाच
verses.devanagari:
मया प्रसन्नेन तवार्जुनेदं
रूपं परं दर्शितमात्मयोगात् ।
तेजोमयं विश्वमनन्तमाद्यं
यन्मे त्वदन्येन न दृष्टपूर्वम्॥
verses.transliteration:
mayā prasannena tavārjunedaṃ rūpaṃ paraṃ darśitamātmayogāt
tejomayaṃ viśvamanantamādyaṃ yanme tvadanyena na dṛṣṭapūrvam
verses.essence: The Blessed Lord says: by my grace, Arjuna, this supreme form was shown to you through my own yoga — made of light, universal, endless, primal — which none before you has ever seen.
verses.translation: O Arjuna, this Cosmic Form has graciously been shown to thee by Me by My own Yogic power; full of splendour, primeval, and infinite, this Cosmic Form of Mine has never been seen before by anyone other than thyself.

pronoun, genitive singular (of you; here 'to you')
past participle, neuter, nominative singular (has been shown)
compound, masculine, ablative singular (through, by means of)

verses.explanation: Krishna gently corrects the frame before granting the retreat: this was prasannena — given out of being *pleased*, a grace, not an ordeal — and tvad-anyena na dṛṣṭa-pūrvam: you are the first. The terror Arjuna wants withdrawn was also the rarest gift ever given; both things are allowed to be true.
verses.connection: Names what 11.9–31 was: unprecedented grace — before honoring the request to veil it.
verses.reflection: Reframe one past ordeal tonight as it may truly have been: a rare grace, fiercely wrapped.
verses.background: Krishna gathers the vision back: this form none have seen before by Veda, sacrifice, or austerity — be not afraid, be not bewildered; behold again My familiar shape. Sanjaya reports the mercy: the Lord shows His gentle human form once more and consoles the terrified archer.
verses.hook: Why did Krishna show Arjuna his cosmic form at all?

views.text: Grace here means the intention to favour Arjuna, and 'by My own yoga' means by the power of His own Godhood; the praise tells Arjuna his ends are already accomplished by this sight.
'Universal' means the form is the Self of the universe, 'primeval' that it is the foundation of all other beings; it is shown to a devotee by the Lord's power of true will.
Asked to withdraw the vision, the Lord first reassures Arjuna; 'other than you' is taken as other than a devotee like you.
The vision was a gift of grace, not punishment, given because Krishna was pleased; it came through Yogamāyā, the divine power by which God does even the impossible.

verses.explanation: The entire religious toolkit is inventoried and set aside: scripture, sacrifice, study, charity, ritual, austerity — none of it purchases this sight. The vision has no price because it was never for sale; it travels only the channel named in 11.47: grace, answering love. The hardest teaching for the spiritually industrious.
verses.connection: Generalizes 11.47: the vision's currency is relationship, not accomplishment — restated at 11.53–54.
verses.reflection: Stop trying to purchase the unpurchasable today — no rite or merit buys the vision; love is the channel.

verses.hook: Can study, ritual or austerity alone earn a vision of God?

refs.note: Says no one can see the Lord without being anointed by his grace, matching Krishna's word that effort alone is not enough.
Relates that Sanjaya received divine sight from his guru Vyāsa, explaining how he too saw the form, and later lost it in grief.

views.text: Study of sacrifices is named apart from Vedic study to mean detailed knowledge of the rites; gifts, rituals like Agnihotra and severe penances like Cāndrāyaṇa all fail to yield this vision.
The means listed fail for anyone who lacks exclusive devotion; 'other than you' means other than one who, like Arjuna, has complete devotion.
The point is that Arjuna, having gained so rare a sight by the Lord's grace alone, has already reached his goal.
Material eyes see only matter; no study, ritual, charity or austerity can show God's divine form. Only when he graces the soul with divine sight can it be seen.

verses.translation: Be not afraid, nor bewildered on seeing such a terrible form of Mine as this; with thy fear dispelled and with a gladdened heart, now behold again this former form of Mine.

verses.explanation: The consolation is given as a series of releases: mā vyathā, no more anguish — the word that has tolled since the worlds first trembled; vyapeta-bhīḥ, fear dismissed; prīta-manāḥ, gladness restored. The Infinite, having shown what it is, now takes responsibility for the showing's wounds. Revelation ends, as it began, in kindness.
verses.connection: The healing words that accompany the form's withdrawal in 11.50.
verses.reflection: After any overwhelming truth, accept the consolation too: be no more afraid; gladness is also commanded.

verses.hook: What does Krishna tell the frightened Arjuna to do now?

views.text: 'That very form' is the earlier one with four hands holding conch, discus and mace, the form dear to Arjuna.
The Lord promises to show the benign form Arjuna was accustomed to, so that the fear and perplexity caused by the terrible form may cease.
Rather than be afraid, Arjuna should feel privileged to have been granted the cosmic vision, and now, free of fear, behold Krishna's personal form again.

आश्वासयामास च भीतमेनं
भूत्वा पुनः सौम्यवपुर्महात्मा॥

verses.essence: Sanjaya says: having spoken thus to Arjuna, Vasudeva showed his own form again; the great Self, becoming once more the gentle-bodied one, comforted him in his terror.
verses.translation: Having thus spoken to Arjuna, Krishna again showed His own form and the great Soul (Krishna), assuming His gentle form, consoled him (Arjuna) who was terrified.

anvaya.form: past participle as adjective, masculine, accusative singular (object)

anvaya.parts: सौम्य (gentle, pleasing) + वपुस् (body): one whose body is gentle
महत् (great) + आत्मन् (self): one whose self is great

verses.explanation: Two words carry the verse: svakaṁ rūpam — his *own* form, as if the universal blaze were the costume and the familiar Krishna the truth — and saumya-vapuḥ, the gentle body, moonlight after the thousand suns. The commentators differ on its shape (Ramanuja and Sridhara see the crowned, four-armed form Arjuna asked for; Shankara simply the form born in Vasudeva's house), but agree on its purpose. The Infinite folds itself back into a friend-sized shape for one reason only: āśvāsayāmāsa, to console.
verses.connection: The visual resolution: the all-form sheathed, the beloved form restored.
verses.reflection: Watch for the gentle form's return after hard revelations — the universe also knows how to console.
verses.background: Krishna gathers the vision back: this form none have seen before by Veda, sacrifice, or austerity — be not afraid, be not bewildered; behold again My familiar shape. Sanjaya reports the mercy: the Lord shows His gentle human form once more and consoles the terrified archer.

views.text: 'His own form' is the form in which He was born in the house of Vasudeva; 'gentle in body' means graceful, serene.
The four-armed form is natural to Krishna even as a man; its two extra arms were hidden at Vasudeva's prayer during Kamsa's rule, and Arjuna's request in 11.46 recalls it.
The form restored is the crowned, four-armed one he had before; 'great-souled' may mean the cosmic one or simply the compassionate one.
Krishna first shows his majestic four-armed form, then returns to his two-armed human form, because Arjuna loved him as a friend and awe-filled reverence could not satisfy that intimate love.

verses.speaker: अर्जुन उवाच
verses.devanagari:

इदानीमस्मि संवृत्तः सचेताः प्रकृतिं गतः॥

verses.essence: Arjuna says: seeing this gentle human form of yours, Janardana, I am now composed — restored to my own nature.
verses.translation: Having seen this Thy gentle human form, O Krishna, now I am composed and am restored to my own nature.

anvaya.parts: स (with) + चेतस् (mind): one who has his mind back

anvaya.form: past participle, masculine, nominative singular (gone to)

verses.explanation: The exhale of the whole chapter: mānuṣaṁ rūpam — the *human* form, and at the sight of it, prakṛtiṁ gataḥ, Arjuna comes back to himself. The verse quietly crowns the incarnation: the form in which God is most bearable, most lovable, most healing, is the one that looks like us. The thousand suns informed him; the human face restored him.
verses.connection: Closure of the vision-arc — before Krishna draws its doctrine in 11.52–55.
verses.reflection: Notice what restores you to yourself — for Arjuna it was a human face. Keep yours near the shaken.
verses.background: Arjuna breathes — 'seeing this human form of Yours, I am composed and restored to my own nature' — and Krishna seals the chapter's meaning: that form is rarely seen, and not by Vedas, austerity, gifts, or rites, but by undivided devotion alone can I be known, seen, and entered. The seed-verse follows: work for Me, love Me, cling to nothing, hate no being.
verses.hook: How does Arjuna feel once he sees Krishna's gentle human form again?

refs.note: Nārada tells Yudhiṣṭhira that the Supreme lives in their house in human guise, like a brother; it shows how familiar Arjuna was with Krishna as kin and friend.

views.text: The form is gentle because it is gracious, as of his friend; seeing it, Arjuna is calm in mind and back to his own nature.
The human form is praised as unique, endowed with grace, tenderness and beauty of infinite excellence.
At the end of withdrawing all things, Brahman rests in a supremely tranquil state; hence at the stage of withdrawal the Lord appears gentle.
Seeing Krishna's familiar two-armed form restores Arjuna's love for him as a friend; he was used to treating the Lord as a brother and companion, so this form brings him back to himself.

verses.explanation: A gentle correction of perspective: the vision Arjuna begged to have *ended* is the one heaven stands in line for — devā api... nityaṁ darśana-kāṅkṣiṇaḥ, the gods themselves wait forever for what he was given between two armies on a workday. Grace is often recognized only in the rearview.
verses.connection: Begins the epilogue-teaching: what the vision was worth, and what alone obtains it.
verses.reflection: Treasure today one ordinary access to the sacred that, unknown to you, the gods envy.

views.text: Though the gods long to see it, they have not seen it as Arjuna has, nor will they.
'This form' is the cosmic one that holds the universe under control and is the origin and foundation of all; no one beholds it by ordinary means.
Krishna stresses that seeing him in his personal two-armed form is so rare that even the gods long for it, so that Arjuna does not let the cosmic vision weaken his love for that form.

verses.explanation: The pillars of religious merit — study, tapas, charity, sacrifice — are dismissed a second time, now with finality and with a new edge: not 'in this form', but 'as you have seen Me'. The repetition from 11.48 is the teaching method: what is said twice at the summit of revelation is meant to be unforgettable. The accounting model of spirituality ends here.
verses.connection: Clears the ground completely for 11.54's single exception.
verses.reflection: Release the spiritual accounting once more: not Vedas, tapas, gifts, nor rites — stop counting today.

views.text: Each means is taken at its fullest: all four Vedas, penances like Cāndrāyaṇa, gifts of cattle, land and gold, sacrifice or worship; none of them shows Him as Arjuna saw.
Read with 11.54: mere study, meditation, gifts and austerities, when empty of devotion to Him, cannot give true knowledge of the Lord.
No amount of Vedic study, austerity or sacrifice can reveal God this way, because he is not known by one's own strength; he is known through the grace that comes to those who love him.

verses.essence: But by devotion that is undivided, Arjuna, I can in this way be known and truly seen — and entered into, O scorcher of foes.
verses.translation: But by single-minded devotion can I, of this Form, be known and seen in reality and also entered into, O Arjuna.

verses.explanation: The single key, after every other door was sealed: bhaktyā tv ananyayā — devotion with no second object, love that does not look sideways. And the three infinitives climb like a staircase: jñātum, to know (from scripture); draṣṭum, to see directly, tattvena, in truth; praveṣṭum — to *enter*. Beyond information, beyond even vision, lies entry: the lover taken into the beloved, which the commentators read as liberation itself. After 11.48 and 11.53 closed every market of works and learning, this is the chapter's final answer to 'who are you?' — the one whom love alone can reach all the way.
verses.connection: The doctrine the whole vision was staged to teach — the keystone of the bhakti chapters.
verses.reflection: Give devotion one undivided hour today — ananya — and aim at all three: know, see, enter.
verses.background: Arjuna breathes — 'seeing this human form of Yours, I am composed and restored to my own nature' — and Krishna seals the chapter's meaning: that form is rarely seen, and not by Vedas, austerity, gifts, or rites, but by undivided devotion alone can I be known, seen, and entered. verses.hook: By what means can God truly be known, seen and entered?

refs.note: Devotion alone leads to God, shows him and brings one to him; God is ruled by devotion, the greatest path.
Krishna tells Uddhava that yoga, philosophy, study, austerity and renunciation do not win him as strong devotion does.
Krishna says he is attained only by devotion, and those who worship him with faith are dear to him.

views.text: Single-minded devotion is that in which nothing but Vasudeva is perceived by any sense; through it He is known from scripture, seen directly, and entered for liberation.
Devotion of extreme ardour is the only means by which the Lord is truly known, seen and entered; the Upanishad's 'whom He chooses, by him He is attained' is cited in support.
For those whose devotion bursts forth with no other object, the Vasudeva-reality descends into realization without effort, through their grasp of the teaching that Vasudeva is all.
'Entering' is glossed as entering by identity (tādātmya), the third step after knowing from scripture and seeing directly; no other means works.
Single-minded devotion, bhakti, is the only means to know and attain God in his personal form, as the scriptures repeat again and again.

verses.explanation: The chapter of overwhelming vision ends in five quiet credentials, fully livable on an ordinary Tuesday: work done as his work, him as the highest goal, love, unclutched hands — and the last, placed where emphasis lives: nirvairaḥ sarva-bhūteṣu, enemy to no being. The man just shown all-devouring Time, and told to fight an army, is given as his final instruction universal friendliness. The vision's last lesson is tenderness.
verses.connection: The chapter's distilled commandment — vision translated into a way of living, bridging into chapter 12's question.
verses.reflection: Live the seed-verse today: His work, His supremacy, His love, no clinging — and enemy to no being.
verses.background: Arjuna breathes — 'seeing this human form of Yours, I am composed and restored to my own nature' — and Krishna seals the chapter's meaning: that form is rarely seen, and not by Vedas, austerity, gifts, or rites, but by undivided devotion alone can I be known, seen, and entered. The seed-verse follows: work for Me, love Me, cling to nothing, hate no being.
verses.hook: What marks a person who truly comes to God?

views.text: A servant works for his master without making him his final goal; this devotee works for the Lord and has Him alone as goal, free of enmity even toward those who do him the utmost harm.
He bears no one hatred because he takes his own sins as the cause of his suffering and knows all beings depend on the Supreme Person.
Introduced as the essence of all scripture and the highest secret; only one so described reaches the Lord, no other.
Seeing the whole world as the Lord's cosmic form, such a devotee cherishes no hatred even toward those who injure him, and so enters the Lord's being.

The chapter closes with five marks of exclusive devotees: they do all work for God, rely on his grace rather than their own practice, love him alone, are free of worldly attachment, and bear no malice to anyone.
